root.note: The god's name is probably built on *wōþuz ‘fury, inspiration’ (Old English wōd ‘mad’). The day name itself is a translation of Latin dies Mercurii.

history: Wednesday is Woden's day. Woden was the highest god of the Anglo-Saxons, the same god the Vikings called Odin. In Old English the day was Wōdnesdæg. The Romans had named the days after their gods and planets, and this day belonged to Mercury: dies Mercurii (French mercredi still shows it). The Germanic peoples took over the system but put in their own gods, and Mercury became Woden. That is why the spelling has a d that most people do not say: /ˈwenzdeɪ/. Dutch woensdag has the same god. German took a different name from Church Latin: Mittwoch, ‘the middle of the week’.
historyEinfach: Wednesday means ‘Woden's day’. Woden was an old god. The Vikings called him Odin. The Romans had a god for every day. This day was for the god Mercury. The old English people put in their own god, Woden. We write Wednesday with a d, but we don't say the d.

elsewhere.text: French mercredi and Spanish miércoles still carry the name of the Roman god Mercury. The Anglo-Saxons translated the idea: they gave the day to Woden, the god they thought was most like Mercury.
Swedish, Danish and Norwegian onsdag is ‘Odin's day’, the Scandinavian twin of Wednesday.
